source_title: A case of humidifier lung with a difficult differential diagnosis from COVID-19
summary_title: A case of humidifier lung with a difficult differential diagnosis from COVID-19
executive_summary: This case report describes a 71-year-old man presenting with cough and dyspnea, initially suspected of having COVID-19 due to diffuse ground-glass opacities (GGOs) on a chest CT scan.  However, his symptoms rapidly improved, prompting further investigation. The patient's history revealed recent use of an ultrasonic humidifier.  A high-resolution CT (HRCT) scan showed ill-defined centrilobular nodules and mosaic attenuation, features more typical of hypersensitivity pneumonitis (HP) than COVID-19.  An inhalation challenge test (ICT) with the humidifier confirmed the diagnosis of humidifier lung, a rare form of HP.  The patient's symptoms, including cough, dyspnea, fever, and hypoxemia, worsened after the ICT, and HRCT revealed re-aggravation of GGOs.  The diagnosis was further supported by the isolation of microorganisms from the humidifier tank water.  The patient was successfully treated with prednisolone and discharged. The report highlights the importance of detailed history-taking, specifically regarding humidifier use, and precise HRCT interpretation in differentiating humidifier lung from COVID-19, particularly given the overlapping clinical and radiological features. The study suggests that the increased use of humidifiers during the COVID-19 pandemic may lead to a rise in humidifier lung cases, necessitating careful diagnostic consideration. The main limitation is that it is a single case report, and the generalizability is limited.
methodological_details: This study is a case report detailing the diagnosis and management of a 71-year-old Japanese man presenting with cough and dyspnea. The patient's history included a 1-week history of cough and dyspnea. He had a 36 pack-year history of cigarette smoking.  The patient denied any pets or recent sick contacts. The patient presented with tachypnea (26 breaths/min) and hypoxemia (SpO2, 93% on room air), without fever, wheezes, lung crackles, or abnormal heart sounds. Laboratory blood tests were performed, including complete blood count and CRP, and KL-6 levels. A chest X-ray and conventional CT scan were performed at an emergency department. The SARS-CoV-2 antigen and PCR tests were performed. The patient was admitted to an isolation ward. Empiric antibiotics (ampicillin/sulbactam and azithromycin) were started. Blood culture and urinary pneumococcal and Legionella antigen tests were performed. After the second negative PCR test for SARS-CoV-2, the patient was moved to a general ward. HRCT images were taken. An inhalational challenge test (ICT) was performed with the humidifier. Pulmonary function tests were performed before and 6 h after the ICT. HRCT was performed 9 h after the ICT. Blood tests were performed on the next day. The humidifier tank water was tested for microorganisms. The patient was started on prednisolone therapy (30 mg/day; 0.5 mg/kg/day). The patient was discharged after 16 days of hospitalization. The study did not specify a preregistration. The study utilized standard medical imaging techniques (chest X-ray, CT, HRCT), laboratory tests (blood tests, PCR), and pulmonary function tests. The study adhered to standard clinical practice for diagnosis and treatment. The study did not mention any ethical considerations or IRB approval.
procedures_architectures: The study describes the clinical presentation, diagnostic process, and treatment of a patient with humidifier lung. The patient underwent a series of diagnostic procedures, including chest X-rays, conventional CT scans, and HRCT scans. The HRCT images were crucial for identifying the characteristic features of HP, such as ill-defined centrilobular nodules and mosaic attenuation. The SARS-CoV-2 PCR test was used to rule out COVID-19. The patient underwent an inhalation challenge test (ICT) using the patient's humidifier. The ICT involved exposing the patient to the humidifier and monitoring for symptoms and physiological changes. Pulmonary function tests were performed before and after the ICT to assess lung function. The humidifier tank water was analyzed to identify potential microorganisms. The patient was treated with prednisolone, which was gradually tapered off. The study does not provide details on specific model architectures or software versions. The study does not describe any novel procedures or architectures. The study relies on standard medical imaging and laboratory techniques.
key_results: The patient presented with cough and dyspnea. Initial chest X-ray and CT scans showed diffuse GGOs. SARS-CoV-2 antigen and PCR tests were negative. The patient's symptoms improved rapidly with initial treatment. HRCT revealed ill-defined centrilobular nodules and mosaic attenuation.  An ICT resulted in cough, dyspnea, fever (37.5°C), and hypoxemia, with an increased alveolar-arterial oxygen tension difference of 53 mmHg. Pulmonary function tests showed a reduction in forced vital capacity from 2.95 l (75.6% of predicted) to 2.22 l (56.9% of predicted) after the ICT. HRCT after the ICT showed re-aggravation of GGOs. Blood tests showed an increased white blood cell count (33,000/μl) and CRP level (9.61 mg/dl) the day after the ICT.  Microorganisms, including Stenotrophomonas maltophilia, Acinetobacter baylyi, and Cladosporium sp., were isolated from the humidifier tank water. The patient was treated with prednisolone and discharged after 16 days. The study did not report any baseline comparisons or effect sizes.
